diagnostic_evidence.quote: the convergence rate of the batch-means estimators is $O(1/\sqrt[4]{t\beta_t})$
Compared to batch-means estimators for first-order methods, our \mbox{estimator} is batch-free and exhibits faster convergence.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 4.1's rate contains the adaptive-stepsize term $\chi_t/\beta_t^{1.5}$. Under the theorem's own condition $\chi>1.5\beta$, this term can decay arbitrarily slowly. For example, with $\beta=0.75$ and $\chi=1.13$ (which satisfies $\chi>1.5\beta=1.125$), $\chi_t/\beta_t^{1.5}=t^{-1.13+1.125}=t^{-0.005}$, while the batch-means rate is $(t\beta_t)^{-1/4}=t^{-(1-0.75)/4}=t^{-0.0625}$. The former is slower than the latter, so the unqualified claim that the proposed estimator is faster is false within the paper's parameter regime.

failure_location.quote: which is slower than that of $\hat{\Xi}_t$~in~\mbox{Theorem}~\ref{sec4:thm1}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add an additional condition on the stepsize parameters (e.g., $\chi\geq 2\beta$) or qualify the comparison to the non-adaptive term, and remove the unqualified faster-convergence claim from the conclusion.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised advantage over batch-means estimators is not universally valid under the theorem's assumptions; the conclusion and comparison section overstate the guaranteed convergence speed.
issues.title: Unqualified faster-convergence claim compared to batch-means estimators
issues.why_classification: The main consistency result remains valid, but a substantive performance advantage is falsely claimed for a nonempty part of the allowed parameter regime; repairing it requires either a new condition or withdrawal of the claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we apply the tower property of conditional expectation to bound $\mE[\uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3}]$ by first conditioning on $\mF_{k-1}$

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 4.1 is proved under Assumptions 1--4. Assumption 3 forces $B_t=\frac1t\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\nabla^2 f(\bx_i;\xi_i)$ to be an average of bounded, strongly convex stochastic Hessians, so $B_t\to\nabla^2 F(\bx_t)\to B^\star$ as $\bx_t\to\bx^\star$. The proof of Lemma 4.1 and the later estimates explicitly use the bound on $\|B_t-B^\star\|$. Thus the theorem does require $B_t$ to converge to the true Hessian. The claim that it applies to conditioned SGD methods where $B_t$ need not approximate the Hessian (e.g., AdaGrad, RMSProp) is unsupported and contradicts the assumptions.

failure_location.quote: Notably, Theorem \ref{sec4:thm1} does~not~\mbox{require}~$B_t$~to~\mbox{converge}~to~the true Hessian $\nabla^2 F(\tx)$, making our analysis directly applicable to conditioned SGD methods.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Remove the claim or state that extending the estimator to conditioned SGD requires a separate analysis and explicit assumptions on the conditioning matrix $B_t$.
issues.overall_effect: The paper overstates the scope of Theorem 4.1, claiming applicability to a broad class of preconditioned first-order methods without proof or appropriate assumptions.
issues.title: False applicability to conditioned SGD without Hessian convergence
issues.why_classification: The core theorem remains correct under its assumptions, but a substantive generalization to conditioned SGD is falsely advertised; repairing it requires either deletion of the claim or a new proof/assumptions.
